sections.h: How the eye forms an image
p: Light from an object enters through the cornea, passes through the aqueous humour, pupil, lens and vitreous humour, and falls on the retina. The cornea and lens together converge the rays to form a real, inverted and diminished image on the retina. The retina changes it into electrical signals carried by the optic nerve to the brain, which interprets the image as upright. The light is bent most at the cornea; the lens does the fine focusing.
In bright light the iris makes the pupil smaller to protect the retina; in dim light it makes the pupil larger to let in more light.

title: Accommodation, Defects of Vision and Care of the Eyes
summary: How the eye focuses on near and far objects, the defects of vision and how lenses correct them, with worked answers to the past questions.

p: Accommodation is the ability of the eye to change the focal length of its lens so that it can focus on near or distant objects. Near object: the ciliary muscles contract, the suspensory ligaments slacken, and the lens becomes thicker and more convex (shorter focal length). Distant object: the ciliary muscles relax, the ligaments pull the lens flatter (longer focal length).

p: A concave lens spreads the rays out slightly before they enter the eye, so that a short-sighted eye brings them to a focus further back, on the retina. A convex lens makes the rays converge a little before entering, so that a long-sighted eye can focus them on the retina.

Do not read in dim light. Never look directly at the sun or at lasers. See an optometrist regularly. Eat foods rich in vitamin A (carrots, spinach, palm oil, liver). Limit screen time and rest your eyes. Wear protective goggles when needed (in the laboratory, welding or grinding). Keep your hands clean to prevent eye infections.

The part controlling the light entering the eye: the iris (C). The defect caused by an eyeball that is too long: short-sightedness (C). Defect corrected by a concave lens: myopia, because the lens diverges the rays so that the image falls on the retina instead of in front of it. A lens for long-sightedness: convex, because it converges the rays so that the image falls on the retina instead of behind it. Astigmatism: corrected with cylindrical lenses that compensate for the uneven curvature of the cornea.

title: Applications of Sound Waves (1): Medicine, Communication and Industry
summary: The properties of sound used in technology, and its applications in medicine, communication and industry.

p: Reflection (echoes) is used in sonar and echolocation. Refraction is used in focusing sound. Diffraction explains how sound spreads from loudspeakers. Interference is used in noise-cancelling headphones. Frequency decides whether sound is audible, ultrasonic or infrasonic. Amplitude and intensity decide loudness and are measured by alarms and sound-level meters.

Diagnostic ultrasound (sonography): sound above 20 kHz (in practice 1 to 20 MHz) is directed into the body, and echoes from tissues of different density are recorded to make an image of the foetus, liver, kidneys or heart. Advantages: safe (it does not use ionising radiation), real-time and painless. Limits: it cannot pass through bones or gas-filled organs.
Therapeutic ultrasound: used in physiotherapy to treat muscle injuries and pain; the vibrations produce gentle heat in tissue. High-intensity focused ultrasound breaks up kidney stones (lithotripsy).

Microphones change sound (mechanical waves) into electrical signals; loudspeakers do the reverse. They are used in phones, public address systems, radios and hearing aids. In telephony, speech is changed into electrical (and then radio) signals for long-distance transmission, as in GSM networks. Voice assistants such as Siri, Alexa and Google Assistant use microphones and software to recognise speech.

Ultrasonic cleaning: high-frequency vibrations in a liquid shake dirt off jewellery, watches and circuit boards. Non-destructive testing (NDT): ultrasonic pulses detect cracks inside aircraft parts, pipelines and bridges; a crack reflects the pulse back sooner. Ultrasonic welding joins plastics and thin metals.

Musical instruments: strings (violin, guitar), air columns (flute, trumpet) and membranes (drums) produce sound by vibration. In studios, microphones, speakers and equalisers adjust the amplitude and frequency to improve sound quality.

Ultrasonic motion detectors send out sound and sense changes in the reflected pattern when something moves. Burglar alarms with sound sensors can react to particular sounds, for example breaking glass.

title: Applications of Sound Waves (2): Nature, Seismology, Sonar and Limits
summary: Echolocation, animal communication, seismic waves, how sonar finds depth and distance, the difference between radar and sonar, and the limits of sound technology.

p: Echolocation: bats, dolphins, whales and some birds send out ultrasonic sounds and listen to the returning echoes to avoid obstacles, find prey and move in the dark. Animal communication: elephants use infrasound that travels long distances; many animals detect thunder or the movement of predators.

Seismic waves are vibrations that travel through the Earth after an earthquake or an explosion. They are mechanical waves like sound, but they are not simply 'sound waves' (some are transverse, and they are mostly infrasonic). Geophones detect them. They are used for earthquake warning systems, volcano monitoring and exploration for oil and minerals: in a seismic survey, reflected waves from underground layers are recorded and used to map rock structure.

SONAR (Sound Navigation and Ranging) uses ultrasonic pulses sent out underwater; the echo's time gives the distance to an object. Depth = v × t ÷ 2, where t is the time for the pulse to go and return and the speed in sea water is about 1,500 m/s. It is used by submarines and ships for navigation, by fishing boats to find shoals of fish, and for mapping the sea floor. Example: an echo returns 0.40 s after a pulse; depth = 1,500 × 0.40 ÷ 2 = 300 m.

img.alt: A ship sending sonar pulses towards a submarine and a target under the water
img.cap: Sonar: a ship detects objects under the water using echoes.

p: Radar uses radio waves (electromagnetic, which travel in air and a vacuum) while sonar uses sound (mechanical). Sonar is used underwater because radio waves are quickly absorbed by water, while sound travels well in it.

Sound cannot travel through a vacuum. It is affected by obstacles, temperature, pressure and humidity. High-frequency ultrasonic equipment is costly. Noise pollution and distortion affect communication. Sound has a shorter range than radio waves or light.

Loud noise from generators, traffic and music can damage hearing (above about 85 dB over long periods), cause stress and disturb sleep. Remedies: silencers, ear protection, soundproofing, planning of noisy activities and rules about noise levels.

title: Electric Charges: Nature and Methods of Charging
summary: What electric charge is, positive and negative charges, the law of charges and charging by friction, conduction and induction.

p: Electric charge is a basic property of matter that makes it feel a force in an electric (and magnetic) field. Its SI unit is the coulomb (C); the symbol is q or Q. Atoms contain protons (positive), electrons (negative) and neutrons (neutral). Protons and electrons carry equal and opposite charges, so an atom is normally neutral. A body becomes charged when it gains or loses electrons: it becomes negative if it gains electrons and positive if it loses them. Protons stay in the nucleus; only electrons move.
Like charges repel; unlike charges attract.

img.alt: A charged ebonite rod near an insulated metal sphere with positive charges on the near side and negative charges on the far side
img.cap: A charged rod redistributes the charge on a nearby metal sphere.

p: When two different materials are rubbed together, electrons move from one to the other. A glass rod rubbed with silk becomes positive (it loses electrons) and the silk negative. An ebonite rod rubbed with fur becomes negative (it gains electrons) and the fur positive. A polythene rod rubbed with a cloth becomes negative.
A charged body touches a neutral conductor. Charge flows between them, and the neutral body gets a charge of the same sign as the charged body.

A charged body is brought near (without touching) a neutral conductor on an insulating stand. Charges in the conductor separate: opposite charge on the near side and like charge on the far side. If the far side is earthed for a moment, the repelled charge flows to earth. When the earth wire is removed and then the charged rod taken away, the conductor is left with a charge of the opposite sign to the rod. Example: a negative rod brings positive charge to the conductor.

img.alt: Charging a conductor positively by induction: a negative rod nearby, free electrons moving away, a brief flow of electrons to earth, and the conductor left positively charged

p: In conduction the charged body touches the conductor and gives it the same sign of charge. In induction there is no contact and the conductor gets the opposite sign, and the charged body does not lose any of its charge.

title: Properties of Charge, Conductors, the Electroscope and Applications
summary: Conservation and quantisation of charge, conductors, insulators and semiconductors, the gold-leaf electroscope, and the uses of static electricity.

p: 1. There are two types only: positive and negative. 2. Charges add algebraically: +5 C and –3 C give +2 C. 3. Conservation of charge: charge can be neither created nor destroyed, only transferred; in an isolated system the total charge stays constant. 4. Quantisation: charge exists in whole-number multiples of the elementary charge e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, so q = ne. Example: q = 5 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. The smallest free charge is 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. 5. Charges exert electrostatic forces on one another, given by Coulomb's law.
The charge carried by 4.0 × 10¹⁹ electrons is q = ne = 4.0 × 10¹⁹ × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 6.4 C. The number of electrons in a charge of 3.2 × 10⁻⁶ C is n = q ÷ e = 3.2 × 10⁻⁶ ÷ 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 2.0 × 10¹³.

Conductors let charge move freely: copper, aluminium, graphite, salt solution. Insulators do not: rubber, glass, plastic, dry wood. Semiconductors conduct poorly when cold but better when heated or when small amounts of other elements are added (doping): silicon and germanium, used in diodes and transistors.

It has a metal cap (disc) joined by a brass rod to a strip of gold leaf inside a glass-fronted case (the earthed metal case or jar). When a charged body touches the cap, charge runs down the rod and into the leaf, and the leaf is repelled from the rod: the leaf rises. Uses: to detect charge; to find the sign of a charge (bring a known charged rod near the cap; if the leaf rises more, the charges are the same; if it falls, they are opposite); to compare quantities of charge roughly (greater divergence, more charge); and to test whether a material is an insulator (a good insulator does not discharge the leaf).

The picture in your lesson note is a poster from a video channel with a watermark, so we do not reproduce it. Draw your own: a brass disc on top of a brass rod, an insulating plug, a glass jar and a gold leaf hanging from the rod.

Photocopiers and laser printers (the drum is charged where toner must stick). Spray painting (paint droplets and the object carry opposite charges, giving an even coat with little waste). Electrostatic precipitators in factory chimneys remove dust and soot. Air purifiers. Lightning is a huge discharge of static charge in clouds; lightning conductors on tall buildings protect them by providing a safe path to earth.

Sparks can ignite petrol vapour, so fuel tankers are earthed with a chain, and a person should not use a phone while fuelling. Lightning kills people on open ground or under tall trees; stay in a building or a car.

title: Fields: Description, Types, Field Lines and Field Strength
summary: What a field is, the gravitational, electric and magnetic fields, how field lines show them, the field strength formulas and the inverse square law.

p: A field is a region of space in which an object experiences a force because of another object, without touching it. Fields explain 'action at a distance'. A scalar field has only magnitude at each point (the temperature in a room); a vector field has magnitude and direction (gravitational, electric and magnetic fields).
Study the table.

head: Field
Source
Acts on
Force
Example
rows: Two bar magnets; a wire and a compass

p: Field lines are imaginary lines that show the direction (and strength) of a field. The direction shows how a small test object would move or be pushed. Where the lines are closer, the field is stronger. Field lines never cross. Electric field lines go from positive to negative charges. Gravitational field lines point towards the mass. Magnetic field lines go from the north pole to the south pole outside the magnet (and continue inside from south to north, forming closed loops).

img.alt: Field lines pointing radially inward toward a mass M, showing that the gravitational field around a mass is radial
img.cap: The gravitational field around a mass is radial.

p: Between two like charges the field lines curve away from each other and there is a neutral point halfway between them where the field is zero.

img.alt: Electric field lines around two positive charges pointing outward and bending away from each other
img.cap: Field of two positive charges (like charges).

p: Two negative charges behave in the same way, but the field lines point inward toward each charge instead of outward.

img.alt: Electric field lines around two negative charges pointing inward and bending away from each other
img.cap: Field of two negative charges (like charges).

p: Magnetic field lines come out of the north pole, curve round and enter the south pole. They are closest together at the poles, where the field is strongest.

img.alt: Magnetic field lines around a bar magnet leaving the north pole and entering the south pole
img.cap: The magnetic field of a bar magnet.

p: Field strength is the force per unit quantity placed in the field. Gravitational: g = F ÷ m = GM ÷ r², in N/kg, with G = 6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ N m²/kg². Electric: E = F ÷ q = kQ ÷ r², in N/C (or V/m), with k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m²/C². Magnetic: B = F ÷ (I L sin θ), in tesla (T). Inverse square law: for gravitational and electric fields, if the distance is doubled, the field strength falls to a quarter.
When several fields act at a point, the resultant field is the vector sum of the separate fields. Examples: two charges, two magnets, or two masses.

title: The Gravitational Field: Newton's Law, Field Strength and Weight
summary: Newton's law of gravitation, gravitational field strength g, weight, the variation of g with height and depth, potential energy, and worked examples with a corrected one.

p: A gravitational field is the region around a mass in which another mass feels an attractive force. It is a vector field, always pointing toward the source mass. It exists around every mass but is noticeable only near big bodies such as the Earth, planets and stars.

img.alt: Gravitational field lines pointing inward to the centre of the Earth, with the planet surface and distances r and 2r marked
img.cap: Field lines around a spherical body point toward its centre.

p: Every particle attracts every other particle with a force directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres: F = Gm₁m₂ ÷ r². G = 6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ N m²/kg² (the universal gravitational constant).

g = F ÷ m = GM ÷ r², in N/kg: the force per unit mass on a small test mass. At the Earth's surface g = GM ÷ R² ≈ 9.8 N/kg (using M = 5.98 × 10²⁴ kg and R = 6.37 × 10⁶ m). Weight W = mg is a force (a vector, in newtons); mass is a scalar, in kilograms, and does not change from place to place.

With height h above the surface: g_h = GM ÷ (R + h)²; g decreases as h increases. With depth d below the surface (assuming constant density): g_d = g₀(1 – d ÷ R); g decreases linearly to zero at the centre.
U = –GMm ÷ r. The negative sign shows that the field is attractive: work must be done to separate the masses. At infinite separation U = 0.

A gravitational field is a vector field, conservative (the work done does not depend on the path), always attractive, obeys the inverse square law, has infinite range and obeys superposition. Applications: weight, satellite orbits, space travel, free fall and projectile motion, tides (the Moon's pull on the oceans), and the structure of stars and galaxies.

2. Force between a star of mass 2.00 × 10³⁰ kg and the Earth (5.98 × 10²⁴ kg), 1.50 × 10⁸ km apart. Convert the distance to metres: r = 1.50 × 10⁸ km = 1.50 × 10¹¹ m. F = Gm₁m₂ ÷ r² = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 5.98 × 10²⁴ × 2.00 × 10³⁰) ÷ (1.50 × 10¹¹)² = 7.977 × 10⁴⁴ ÷ 2.25 × 10²² = 3.55 × 10²² N. (The lesson note forgot to change kilometres to metres and got 3.55 × 10²⁸ N, which is a million times too large.)
3. The force between two point masses is 10⁻⁴ N at 0.18 m. At 0.06 m: F ∝ 1/r², so F₂ = F₁ × (0.18 ÷ 0.06)² = 10⁻⁴ × 9 = 9 × 10⁻⁴ N.
4. g at 4 m from 10 kg: g = 6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ × 10 ÷ 4² = 4.17 × 10⁻¹¹ N/kg (tiny, which is why we do not feel the pull of everyday objects).
5. A 60.0 kg object feels a force of 1.002 × 10² N on the Moon: g = F ÷ m = 100.2 ÷ 60 = 1.67 N/kg.
A man weighs 800 N on Earth: his mass = 800 ÷ 9.8 = 81.6 kg. On the Moon: W = 81.6 × 1.63 = 133 N.
A 50 kg body where g = 9.8 N/kg weighs W = 50 × 9.8 = 490 N.
Astronauts in orbit are still pulled by gravity (g is about 8.7 N/kg at 400 km), but the station and the astronauts are in free fall around the Earth together, so they feel weightless.
